repositories.name: ds-harness-remote
repositories.description: 基于 DeepSeek Harness 插件机制构建的远程访问方案，通过低延迟、端到端加密的 P2P 网络，支持使用 PC、移动端 和 Web 随时访问本地设备上的DSH 、CodeX、Cursor、Claude Code等工作区。 (Built on DeepSeek Harness plugins, this low-latency, end-to-end encrypted P2P solution lets PC, mobile, and web clients access local DSH, Codex, Cursor, and Claude Code workspaces.)
repositories.readme:
English  ·  中文  ·  日本語  ·  Documentation  ·  Web  ·  Android  ·  iOS

Self-hosting  ·  npm  · 

## Connect once. Ready whenever you are. Continue using your DeepSeek Harness instance from a phone, computer, or browser. Return to the same Harness session from whichever device is with you. Harness keeps running on your work computer, with the same workspaces, tools, and project setup. DS Harness Remote is simply another window into that environment. The DeepSeek Harness desktop edition is supported. Install the latest release: `ds-harness-remote@0.6.3` ## Features - Access your local Harness instance remotely from the web, a PC, or a mobile device: DSH first, with Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity support too. - DeepSeek Harness Desktop is ready to use after installation, with its native interface and no separate desktop conversation UI. - Create workspaces, configure models, and switch conversation models with the same smooth workflow as local use. - No public listening port or public IP is required on the Harness Host. Connect from anywhere with internet access over a bidirectional end-to-end encrypted channel. - Prefer P2P connections, use TURN relay nodes worldwide, and fall back to multiple Server Relays when needed. - Access workspace files, read-only previews, remote terminals, and authorized local development-service previews through the native Harness sidebar. - Remote Tool context injection supports Host and workspace discovery, Harness session creation and management, history reading, waiting for execution, interruption requests, and authorized file transfers. [Details](packages/plugin/README.md#remote-agent-tools). - Alongside DeepSeek Harness, access native workspaces for Codex, Cursor, Google Antigravity, Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code, Hermes Agent, and other tools through ACP integrations, with remote file browsing and terminals. - Clients are available across Android, iOS, Web, and native DSH. - Multiple clients can connect to the same Harness Host simultaneously, with RPC calls and streams isolated per connection. ## Contents - [Connect once. Ready whenever you are](#connect-once-ready-whenever-you-are) - [Features](#features) - [Supported clients](#supported-clients) - [Install](#install) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Screenshots](#screenshots) - [How it works](#how-it-works) - [Experimental ACP workspaces](#experimental-acp-workspaces) - [End-to-end encryption](#end-to-end-encryption) - [Network and transport](#network-and-transport) - [Security](#security) - [FAQ](#faq) - [Documentation](#documentation) - [Links](#links) - [Star History](#star-history) - [Project status and trademarks](#project-status-and-trademarks) - [License](#license) ## Supported clients | Client | Form | Status | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | DSH Desktop plugin | Remote sidebar | Supported | Install `ds-harness-remote@0.6.3`; this computer can also be the Host | | Web | Browser page | Supported | Open [https://dsh.r2049.cn](https://dsh.r2049.cn); reuses the native Harness interface | | Android | Native app | Supported | Download the APK from [Releases](https://github.com/liguobao/ds-harness-remote/releases/latest); see the [Android guide](apps/android/README.md) | | DSH Go | A standout app by ccch1mneyyy | Supported | See [ccch1mneyyy/dsh-go: an Android client for DeepSeek Harness. Run it directly on your phone or control DSH on your computer remotely.](https://github.com/ccch1mneyyy/dsh-go) | | iOS | TestFlight beta | Beta | Not publicly released; see [issue #20](https://github.com/liguobao/ds-harness-remote/issues/20) | | Browser extension | Chrome | Entry point only | Exchanges an already signed-in Web authorization for a separate device credential, lists online Hosts and opens the same-origin Remote Web; it does not host a conversation UI | | dsh-TUI | Terminal-only CLI | Planned | Integration is not part of this release and returns in a later version; the installer never creates a Web service for it automatically | | Linux | Cloud server | Supported | Sign in on the [official website](https://dsh.r2049.cn/) for unattended installation with a single command and no configuration. | Several clients can connect to the same Host at once; RPC calls and streams are isolated per connection. ## Install ### DeepSeek Harness Desktop support Open **Extensions / Plugin management** in DeepSeek Harness Desktop, choose installation from npm, and enter this package: `ds-harness-remote@0.6.3` Restart Desktop afterward. Its official `dsh` launcher can also install the pinned package with `dsh plugin --profile desktop add -w ds-harness-remote@0.6.3`. On DSH 0.2.2+, npm installations support version checks and updates in Plugin management, with an attempt to restore the previous version if hot updating fails. GitHub and local link installations must switch to npm first; see [online updates](docs/installation.md#online-updates-in-dsh-plugin-management). ### Linux one-command installation Visit [https://dsh.r2049.cn](https://dsh.r2049.cn/), sign in, and obtain an installation authorization code to install with one command. ### Native Android client Keep conversations connected across multiple workspaces at once, and use **Bot mode**, powered by [Fei2411/DS-Bot](https://github.com/Fei2411/DS-Bot). Download the latest APK from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/liguobao/ds-harness-remote/releases/latest), and sign in to the same account to see your Hosts. ## DSH Go — DeepSeek Harness in your pocket: run it locally on your phone or control your computer remotely. [ccch1mneyyy/dsh-go](https://github.com/ccch1mneyyy/dsh-go) has built-in support for the ds-harness-remote protocol. You can run DeepSeek Harness locally on your phone or connect to your computer remotely. After installing the ds-harness-remote plugin in DSH Go on your phone, you can also connect to the phone’s DSH from your computer or the web and use Mobile Use seamlessly. ### iOS client - [Join the beta](https://github.com/liguobao/ds-harness-remote/issues/20) ## Quick start 1. Open **Remote** from the DeepSeek Harness sidebar. 2. Choose Zhihu, GitHub, or Google authorization, or sign in with an account and password. Account registration requires an invitation code; email the repository author to request one. 3. On another device, install the same plugin in DeepSeek Harness and sign in as described in steps 1–2. Alternatively, use Remote Web, iOS, Android, or DSH Go directly without installing a plugin. 4. Select an online Host, then choose an existing workspace or browse remote directories to open one. By default, Remote uses this project's hosted Server at [https://dsh.r2049.cn](https://dsh.r2049.cn). For self-hosting, use the repository's [minimal Server](apps/server/README.md). The current version includes WebRTC LAN/P2P/TURN coordination (TURN requires your own coturn deployment) and an encrypted Relay Server, but does not provide the full hosted Remote Web experience. ## Screenshots ### Desktop On another computer, select an online Host and open its workspace. The workspace opens in the native Harness interface, with the active Host and encrypted connection status in the header.

To prevent this computer from controlling other Hosts, open the Host list at [https://dsh.r2049.cn/](https://dsh.r2049.cn/) and enable **Controlled only**. This device will no longer see other devices under your account, while Web and other clients can still connect to it remotely. ### Android Use text or image prompts, switch models, and access supported workspace files and terminals. The interface follows the system language and supports English, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, German, and French. In language settings, tap “More ...” to show all languages. See the [Android guide](apps/android/README.md) for details.

Mobile Settings includes a global **Compact conversations** switch, off by default and applied when a conversation is next opened. Supporting Hosts reduce historical tool details while preserving messages and tool status. Turn the setting off and reopen the conversation to load full history. ## How it works ```text DSH Desktop / Remote Web / Android ↔ authenticated, end-to-end encrypted channel Remote Plugin on the Host ↔ supported Harness or optional Codex workspace support Harness sessions/workspaces or Codex projects ``` The Harness Host does not need a public listening port. Connect from anywhere with internet access over ds-harness-remote’s bidirectional end-to-end encrypted channel. The client switches to the selected Host’s native Harness API, keeping the original workspaces, tools, and permission flows on that computer. You can also edit Harness and plugin settings on the remote host. Available options depend on which settings Harness and each plugin expose through the official settings API. ## Experimental ACP workspaces The Host runs local ACP-capable Agents and forwards prompts, streamed replies, and approvals through ds-harness-remote. Each Agent keeps its own workspaces and sessions; only session translation for DSH is performed, without writing to Harness storage. Supported backends: - **Codex** — connects through App Server, using the shared workspace entry. - **Cursor** — connects through the CLI's ACP interface. - **Antigravity (AGY)** — connects through an adapter for its stream-json CLI. - **Pi Agent (experimental)** — automatically detected after installing and configuring Pi and `pi-acp`; can be disabled in settings. Tools run with Host-user permissions, without per-tool confirmation by default. - **OpenCode** — connects through `opencode acp`, with workspaces and history. Session archiving requires a build with the authenticated API; unarchive is not yet available. - **Claude** — connects through a locally authorized `claude-agent-acp`; enable it in settings. Supports text and approvals; images are not yet supported. - **Hermes** — connects through `hermes acp`; enable it in settings. Supports text, images, streamed output, approvals, and model selection. Claude and Hermes also support direct file and terminal access, subject to the Host's workspace boundaries and terminal settings. Setup and adapter development: [Agent workspace integration guide](docs/acp-integration.md). Model selection for Cursor, Claude, Hermes, Pi, OpenCode, and AGY on Desktop/Android uses the Host's actual model catalog as determined by the Agent’s ACP interface. Reasoning effort options depend on what the backend provides. Cursor uses a separate process per session, so model changes do not affect other conversations. ## End-to-end encryption Harness business traffic is encrypted on the Client and decrypted only by the selected Host using the fixed `Noise_IK_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256` suite. Connections must pass both same-account membership and locally pinned device identity key checks. The service can coordinate connections and observe necessary network metadata, but it cannot read session messages, prompts, tool output, workspace paths, or remote file contents. See [End-to-end encryption](docs/end-to-end-encryption.md) for the handshake, key lifecycle, visible metadata, replay protection, and security limits. ## Network and transport The Host opens outbound connections only; it does not listen on a public port or require router port forwarding. Remote negotiates paths in the order `LAN -> P2P -> TURN -> Relay`. When WebRTC is unavailable or cannot connect, it falls back to the encrypted WebSocket Relay. Every path carries the same Noise ciphertext and keeps the same Host/Client identity boundary. See [Network and transport](docs/network.md) for the topology, control and data planes, NAT behavior, fallback, reconnect semantics, and current validation status. ## Security - On LAN and P2P paths, data bypasses the Server except for connection coordination. TURN uses the open-source coturn server; Relay mode forwards traffic over WebSocket. - Session traffic is end-to-end encrypted. The service relays ciphertext without storing session plaintext or device private keys. - Server membership and the Host's locally pinned peer identity must both authorize a connection. - [Remote Tools injection](docs/remote-tools.md) — optional `remote_*` session tools; enabled by default and configurable in detailed Remote settings. - Interactive terminals use the Host-local `terminal.enabled` switch (on by default). They run as the Host user, independently of Agent approvals. - General tool RPC and remote desktop are not exposed. - The workspace picker lists folders only and returns bounded, read-only directory metadata. - Remote file preview cannot write, delete, upload, execute, or open a path in an external application. - Codex Remote / Agent ACP is optional, can be disabled, and follows the same encrypted Host permission boundary as the rest of Remote. - Removing a device revokes its credentials, membership, and active Remote connections. ## FAQ **Do I need a public IP or port forwarding?** No. The Host only opens outbound connections and never listens on a public port. **Can the service read my conversations?** No. The service relays ciphertext only. Routing, authorization, presence and rate limiting require control metadata such as account and device ownership, online status, connection times and `connectionId`; prompts, conversation content, tool input and output, workspace paths and file preview contents stay unreadable. **Which machine can act as a Host?** Any signed-in Harness instance with the Remote plugin installed can act as a Host, whether on Windows, macOS, Linux, or even DSH Go. **Can several devices connect to one Host at the same time?** There is currently no limit on concurrent client connections, with RPC calls and streams isolated per connection. **Which Harness versions are supported?** The current baseline is `dsh-v0.2.2-rc.1`; `dsh-v0.2.1-rc.5` and `0.2.0` rc.2 / rc.1 remain compatible on the same official carrier. See the [compatibility guide](docs/compatibility.md). Harness `0.1.1-rc.2` ApiProxy support has been removed from the Host plugin, its bundled Remote client, and Android. Use a Host with the official Typert Remote carrier; Hosts that only provide ApiProxy or lack capability discovery are rejected, with no fallback. CodeX/ACP keep their independent data planes, and Desktop projections use Typert in memory. **Why does the Linux installer require root?** It configures a systemd system service, so the Host, Agent tools and remote terminals run with root privileges. Only expose it to trusted accounts. **Can I install the iOS app directly?** It is in TestFlight beta today and not publicly released; see [issue #20](https://github.com/liguobao/ds-harness-remote/issues/20). **How is this different from frp, a tunnel, or remote desktop?** Conventional server-based TCP port forwarding routes traffic through a Server, making its bandwidth a potential bottleneck. This project probes four connection modes in sequence to establish P2P connections even in complex network environments. Remote desktop captures the entire computer screen and reproduces it on the client, placing demands on upload and download bandwidth as well as computer performance. This project encrypts and transmits only the messages needed by the native Harness conversation interface. General tool RPC and desktop control are not exposed, and permissions and approvals remain on the Host. Tailscale, CF Turn, and UU Remote are also excellent solutions; choose whichever fits your needs. ## Recommended plugins ### Intelligent UI [Intelligent UI](https://github.com/dreamfarer-space/deepseek-harness-intelligent-ui) lets models answer with cards, tables, charts, and forms. The Android client renders them natively and lists the plugin under **Plugins → Remote ready**, where you can enable or disable it and edit live settings. ### [Fei2411/DS-Bot](https://github.com/Fei2411/DS-Bot) DS Bot is a bot plugin for DeepSeek Harness (dsh) that turns dsh into a bot. You can chat and work with the bots you create. ## Documentation - [Plugin guide](packages/plugin/README.md) - [Installation guide](docs/installation.md) - [Codex Remote technical notes](docs/codex-remote.md) - [ACP Remote / Agent adapter notes](docs/acp-remote.md) - [Documentation index](docs/README.md) - [End-to-end encryption](docs/end-to-end-encryption.md) - [Network and transport](docs/network.md) - [Remote Protocol](docs/protocol.md) - [Development status and roadmap](docs/TODO.md) - [Changelog](docs/CHANGELOG.md) - [Privacy policy](docs/PRIVACY.md) - [Android guide](apps/android/README.md) - The current development baseline is `dsh-v0.2.2-rc.1`; validation scope is documented in [the compatibility guide](docs/compatibility.md). ## Links - Friendly link: [DSH Go](https://github.com/ccch1mneyyy/dsh-go) — DeepSeek Harness in your pocket: run it locally on your phone or control your computer remotely. Remote integration is available. - Friendly link: [dsh-TUI](https://github.com/ccch1mneyyy/dsh-TUI) — terminal-first Harness client; Remote integration is planned for a later release. - Friendly link: [LINUX DO](https://linux.do/) - Friendly link: [Cyber Liu Kanshan](https://kanshan.r2049.cn/) ## Star History ## Project status and trademarks This is an independent community project and is not an official DeepSeek product. DeepSeek and related names and marks belong to their respective owners. ## License [MIT](packages/plugin/LICENSE)

repositories.readme:
# voxl

[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/voxl-server.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/voxl-server)

Low-latency desktop streaming for the browser, written in Rust. voxl streams an X11
display, a Mac's screen or a Windows desktop as H.264 over a WebSocket to a small web
client that decodes with WebCodecs, with input, clipboard, audio, microphone, file and
folder transfer and dynamic resolution.

## Quick start

```sh
cargo install voxl-server   # needs x264, libyuv, Opus, PulseAudio and esbuild (see Usage)
DISPLAY=:1 voxl             # streams display :1 and prints a link that signs you in
```

Open the link it prints. On a Mac or a Windows PC, `voxl` streams that machine's own
screen instead; see [macOS](#macos) and [Windows](#windows).

## Benchmarks

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/acdf3f31-64fc-4acf-b5c5-ff173d7100a8

In every test below voxl averages 60 FPS with a median latency of 12–99 ms; noVNC
averages under 8 FPS.

A 16 vCPU AMD EPYC 9334 VM (no GPU), 2560x1600 Xvfb desktop, same workloads, each
stream decoded by a native client that reads a pixel marker drawn into the content.
Cells are FPS (worst second), then latency p50/p99 from the content being drawn to the
frame being decoded. voxl's column is its best run of each test. To reproduce, see
[`bench/`](bench/README.md).

| Test                           | voxl                       | [selkies](https://github.com/selkies-project/selkies) | [KasmVNC](https://github.com/kasmtech/KasmVNC) | [Neko](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko) | [Neko, tuned](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko) | [Sunshine](https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine) | [Sunshine, tuned](https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine) | [noVNC](https://github.com/novnc/noVNC) | [Daytona](https://www.daytona.io) |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Chromium scroll, LAN           | **60.1 (59.7), 55/60 ms**  | 56.8 (54.0), 85/106 ms                                | 51.7 (39.5), 99/135 ms                         | 25.0 (23.7), 156/217 ms               | 53.9 (49.9), 128/155 ms                      | 28.3 (23.5), 88/115 ms                             | 48.5 (44.0), 94/117 ms                                    | 6.7 (6.3), 198/301 ms                   | 5.2 (2.5), 306/713 ms             |
| Scroll, 10 Mbps / 40 ms RTT    | **60.0 (59.4), 82/94 ms**  | 55.6 (47.7), 152/261 ms                               | 8.3 (7.4), 229/249 ms                          | 24.6 (14.9), 221/737 ms               | 46.3 (40.3), 606/831 ms                      | 27.9 (25.3), 160/179 ms                            | 51.3 (47.5), 147/162 ms                                   | 2.6 (2.4), 426/678 ms                   | 1.9 (1.6), 617/798 ms             |
| Scroll, 5 Mbps / 60 ms RTT     | **60.1 (59.7), 99/109 ms** | 27.9 (19.6), 2.7/3.7 s                                | 4.9 (3.6), 306/415 ms                          | 21.7 (3.8), 1.2/3.6 s                 | stalls                                       | 29.6 (21.9), 178/207 ms                            | 44.5 (35.2), 164/191 ms                                   | 1.6 (1.4), 637/937 ms                   | 1.1 (0.9), 1.1/1.2 s              |
| 1080p animation, LAN           | **60.1 (59.9), 12/16 ms**  | 58.7 (55.9), 31/48 ms                                 | 56.7 (51.6), 51/82 ms                          | 24.8 (23.6), 122/202 ms               | 55.6 (50.0), 54/82 ms                        | 27.1 (22.7), 69/91 ms                              | 45.6 (40.3), 42/57 ms                                     | 7.7 (7.2), 149/210 ms                   | 10.5 (8.8), 138/209 ms            |
| Animation, 10 Mbps / 40 ms RTT | **60.1 (59.5), 46/71 ms**  | 39.3 (31.8), 2.3/3.1 s                                | 52.9 (49.2), 76/115 ms                         | 25.1 (9.1), 295/962 ms                | 33.3 (25.4), 4.0/7.1 s                       | 29.7 (26.0), 108/125 ms                            | 51.1 (44.6), 86/107 ms                                    | 5.8 (5.2), 160/226 ms                   | 7.4 (7.0), 154/213 ms             |
| Animation, 5 Mbps / 60 ms RTT  | **60.0 (58.8), 66/92 ms**  | 18.4 (15.3), 2.2/4.3 s                                | 34.1 (26.4), 104/156 ms                        | 15.2 (8.6), 5.0/9.4 s                 | stalls                                       | 34.7 (25.4), 123/143 ms                            | 45.5 (40.9), 114/131 ms                                   | 5.1 (4.7), 174/240 ms                   | 5.8 (4.4), 189/252 ms             |

| Server CPU, X server + streamer (cores)                   | idle | 1080p animation  | scroll           | full screen      |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| voxl                                                      | 0.00 | 1.39             | 1.33             | 1.68             |
| [selkies](https://github.com/selkies-project/selkies)     | 1.29 | not measured     | 1.54             | 1.80             |
| [KasmVNC](https://github.com/kasmtech/KasmVNC)            | 0.00 | 1.97             | 2.07             | 1.82 (at 34 FPS) |
| [Neko](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko)                     | 1.63 | 2.50 (at 25 FPS) | 2.20 (at 25 FPS) | 2.46 (at 23 FPS) |
| [Neko](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko), tuned              | 1.90 | 2.28             | 2.30             | 2.52             |
| [Sunshine](https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine)        | 2.10 | 2.34 (at 27 FPS) | 2.24 (at 28 FPS) | 2.35 (at 25 FPS) |
| [Sunshine](https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine), tuned | 2.84 | 3.07 (at 46 FPS) | 3.14 (at 49 FPS) | 3.22 (at 47 FPS) |
| [noVNC](https://github.com/novnc/noVNC)                   | 0.01 | 0.55 (at 8 FPS)  | 0.58 (at 7 FPS)  | 0.64 (at 6 FPS)  |
| [Daytona](https://www.daytona.io) (1 CPU limit)           | 0.02 | 0.82 (at 10 FPS) | 0.53 (at 5 FPS)  | 0.81 (at 9 FPS)  |

- **selkies:** [selkies](https://github.com/selkies-project/selkies) with picom running.
- **KasmVNC:** 1.4.0 with a 60 FPS cap, JPEG/WebP quality 8–9 and video mode, no
  compositor.
- **Neko:** [m1k1o/neko](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko) 3.2 with its defaults (VP8, 25
  FPS). **Neko, tuned** captures at 60 FPS and encodes with x264 `ultrafast`/
  `zerolatency` at up to 30 Mbps, like voxl. Neither adapts its bitrate (Neko's
  estimator is off by default), so on slow links frames queue up; "stalls" means no
  frame arrived in 20 s.
- **Sunshine:** [Sunshine](https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine) 2025.628 streaming to
  Moonlight ([moonlight-embedded](https://github.com/moonlight-stream/moonlight-embedded)
  2.7, patched to hand frames to the benchmark client). Sunshine is built around GPU
  capture and encoding; without a GPU it falls back to copying the X11 screen and x264,
  so these numbers show it on a GPU-less VM like the other tests, not on the gaming PC
  it's made for. **Sunshine** runs its defaults (`superfast` on 2 threads) at Moonlight's
  default 40 Mbps; **Sunshine, tuned** uses `ultrafast` on 4 threads at 30 Mbps, like
  voxl (8 or 16 threads did no better). Neither reaches 60 FPS on this VM, and it keeps
  working while the screen is still (its idle CPU). Moonlight doesn't adapt its bitrate,
  so on slow links it's set to 80% of the link. Its CPU was measured in a later session,
  where voxl used 1.74, 1.65 and 1.99 cores on the same workloads.
- **noVNC:** x11vnc and noVNC as [E2B Desktop](https://github.com/e2b-dev/desktop)
  and Daytona ship them (`-forever -wait 50 -shared`, Tight encoding). x11vnc polls the
  screen, which caps it at 6–8 FPS.
- **Daytona:** a default sandbox (1 CPU, x11vnc and noVNC at 2560x1600) streamed
  through Daytona's signed preview proxy, about 12 ms away, which its latency includes.
  The workloads run inside the sandbox, sharing its CPU, and slow links are added on top
  of that internet path.
- **Links:** a bottleneck with a deep queue: a TCP proxy for the WebSocket servers, and
  `tc netem` for Neko's WebRTC media and Sunshine's video (UDP). None of them drop
  packets, where UDP with error correction would have the edge.

## Usage

Build (needs Rust, pkg-config, clang, x264, libyuv, libopus, libpulse and esbuild;
`nix-shell` provides them all):

```sh
nix-shell
cargo build --release
```

Or install it from [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/voxl-server) with the same
libraries on your system (the crate is `voxl-server`, the binary is `voxl`):

```sh
cargo install voxl-server
```

Run it against an X display, then open the link it prints (`?stats` adds an FPS
overlay):

```sh
DISPLAY=:1 ./target/release/voxl --port=6901
# prints: open http://localhost:6901/?token=4f1c… to sign in
```

Start Xvfb with `-shmem` for zero-copy capture, and use the patched Xvfb
(`nix-build -E 'with import <nixpkgs> {}; callPackage ./xvfb.nix {}'`) for smooth
scrolling. voxl accepts selkies' command-line flags; other selkies flags are ignored.
`voxl --help` lists every flag with its default, and `voxl --version` prints the version.

| Flag                                                           | Default                            |                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--addr`, `--port`                                             | `0.0.0.0`, `6901`                  | listen address                                                                                                    |
| `--title`                                                      | `Voxl Computer Stream`             | the page's title: the browser tab, and the app's name if a viewer installs it                                     |
| `--favicon`                                                    | voxl's icon                        | the tab's icon: an `.ico`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp` or `.svg` file                                                 |
| `--enable-basic-auth`                                          | `true`                             | ask for a password (see [Login](#login)); `false` serves without one                                              |
| `--basic-auth-password`                                        | `VOXL_PASSWORD`, else made up      | the password                                                                                                      |
| `--basic-auth-user`                                            | any                                | the user name a browser's sign-in has to give                                                                     |
| `--framerate`                                                  | `60`                               | max frames per second (`60-60` style ranges accepted)                                                             |
| `--preset`                                                     | `ultrafast`                        | x264 preset                                                                                                       |
| `--encoder-threads`                                            | `min(4, ncpu/4)`                   | x264 sliced threads                                                                                               |
| `--crf`                                                        | `24`                               | base quality                                                                                                      |
| `--max-kbps` / `--video-bitrate`                               | `30000`                            | adaptive bitrate ceiling                                                                                          |
| `--min-kbps`                                                   | `2000`                             | adaptive bitrate floor                                                                                            |
| `--paintover-crf`, `--paintover-burst`, `--paintover-delay-ms` | `16`, `3`, `150`                   | sharpening when the screen goes still                                                                             |
| `--enable-clipboard`                                           | `true`                             | `true`, `in`, `out` or `false`                                                                                    |
| `--audio-enabled`, `--audio-device-name`, `--audio-bitrate`    | `true`, `output.monitor`, `128000` | desktop audio                                                                                                     |
| `--enable-resize`, `--resize-scale`                            | `false`, `1.5`                     | desktop follows the viewer's window; desktop pixels per CSS pixel                                                 |
| `--microphone-enabled`, `--microphone-fifo`                    | `false`, `/tmp/voxl-mic.fifo`      | browser microphone into the FIFO a PulseAudio pipe source reads                                                   |
| `--round-corners`                                              | `0` (off)                          | corner radius in pixels for top-level windows                                                                     |
| `--round-windows`                                              | none                               | `title:radius,...` rounds windows with that title, docks included                                                 |
| `--adaptive-threads`                                           | `false`                            | encode on one thread, fanning out only under sustained heavy motion                                               |
| `--stripes`                                                    | `1`                                | encode the screen as N independent horizontal streams (experimental)                                              |
| `--scroll-px-per-notch`                                        | `180`                              | desktop pixels one wheel notch scrolls (calibrates smooth scrolling)                                              |
| `--file-transfers`                                             | `upload,download`                  | `upload`, `download`, both, or `none`                                                                             |
| `--read-only`                                                  | `false`                            | viewers only watch: input, clipboard writes, the microphone, uploads and resizing (`--enable-resize`) are refused |
| `--allowed-hosts`                                              | none                               | host names to answer for besides IP addresses and `localhost` (`.example.com` covers subdomains, `*` any)         |
| `--allowed-origins`                                            | none                               | other sites whose pages may connect, such as a page that embeds voxl's client (`*` any site)                      |
| `--files-root`                                                 | `$HOME`                            | folder the Files panel can see; nothing outside it is reachable                                                   |
| `--upload-dir`                                                 | `Downloads`                        | folder (under the root) the panel opens and uploads into; created on first upload                                 |
| `--max-upload-mb`                                              | `0` (no limit)                     | largest accepted upload                                                                                           |
| `--max-record-seconds`                                         | `300`                              | longest recording (`/record`)                                                                                     |
| `--convert-threads`, `--coalesce-us`                           | `4`, `0`                           | tuning                                                                                                            |

### Login

voxl asks for a password before it shows the desktop or takes input, files or API
calls. Give it one with `--basic-auth-password` or `VOXL_PASSWORD`; otherwise it makes
one up when it starts and prints a link that signs you in. There are three ways in:

- **The link**: `http://host:6901/?token=<password>`. The page passes the password on to
  its own connections, so the link also works as an iframe's `src`.
- **The browser's sign-in prompt**, which voxl's page brings up: any user name (unless
  `--basic-auth-user` names one) and the password. Password managers offer to save it.
- **For programs**: `Authorization: Bearer <password>`, or `curl -u :<password>`.

The page's scripts and `/healthz` load without it. If voxl sits behind a proxy that signs
people in itself, `--enable-basic-auth=false` turns voxl's login off.

### Hosts and origins

voxl only answers requests for an IP address or `localhost`, and only from its own page.
That keeps out other web pages, which browsers let connect to any address, including
pages whose domain is pointed at voxl's address (DNS rebinding). To reach voxl under a
host name, such as through a proxy or as `my-pc.local`, name it with `--allowed-hosts`.
To let a page on another site connect, name that site with `--allowed-origins`.
Programs that aren't browsers (curl, scripts, agents) send no `Origin` and connect as
usual. A refused request gets a 403 that names the flag to add.

### For agents and scripts

Screenshots and recordings (start voxl with `VOXL_PASSWORD` set, and send it along):

```sh
# the screen as a PNG
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -o shot.png localhost:6901/screenshot
# an MP4 of the next 10 s
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -o clip.mp4 "localhost:6901/record?seconds=10"
# or start...
id=$(curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -s -X POST localhost:6901/record/start | jq .id)
# ...and stop when done
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -o clip.mp4 -X POST "localhost:6901/record/stop?id=$id"
```

A recording is the H.264 voxl already sends to viewers, saved as MP4 without encoding
it again, so it costs no extra CPU. It doesn't include the cursor (viewers draw it), and
a resize ends it.

`/wait` returns when the screen settles or changes, so an agent doesn't have to sleep
after every action and hope it was long enough:

```sh
# once nothing changed for 300 ms
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" localhost:6901/wait
# still for 1 s, giving up after 30 s
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" "localhost:6901/wait?idle=1000&timeout=30000"
# the first change in that rectangle
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" "localhost:6901/wait?change&region=0,0,800,600"
# {"changed":true,"timed_out":false,"seq":812,"waited_ms":340}
```

`idle` (ms, default 300) is how long the screen has to stay still, counted from the
request at the earliest so an action just taken has time to show; `change` returns at
the first change instead. `region=x,y,w,h` only watches that rectangle (to the 16-pixel
block) and `timeout` (ms, default 10000) gives up. `changed` says whether anything
changed while waiting. A change can land before the request does, so to wait for what an
action caused, pass `since` the `seq` of an earlier `/wait` or the `X-Voxl-Seq` header of
a screenshot: `/wait?change&since=812` returns at once if anything changed after it. A
blinking text caret redraws about twice a second, so keep `idle` under 500 ms or leave
the caret out of `region`. voxl already knows which parts of the screen change (XDamage,
ScreenCaptureKit and DXGI report them), so waiting needs no screenshots or polling.

### macOS

voxl also streams a Mac's own screen, with every feature of the Linux version
(ScreenCaptureKit capture, CGEvent input, NSPasteboard clipboard, system audio).

```sh
brew install x264 opus pkgconf esbuild
cargo build --release
./target/release/voxl --port=6901
```

Open the link it prints. On a Mac voxl listens on `127.0.0.1` unless `--addr` says
otherwise, since the stream is your whole screen. macOS asks voxl (or the terminal that
starts it) for Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions. For the microphone,
install a loopback device (`brew install blackhole-2ch`) and pick it as the input in the
apps that should hear you.

| macOS flag             | Default                     |                                                                                        |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--display`            | main display                | display to stream: an index (0 is the main display) or a display ID; logged at startup |
| `--capture-scale`      | native, within the budget   | streamed pixels per point                                                              |
| `--max-capture-pixels` | `4096000` (2560x1600)       | pixel budget for the automatic scale: x264's cost grows with area                      |
| `--microphone-device`  | first loopback device found | output device (name or prefix) to play the browser microphone into                     |
| `--resize-scale`       | the capture scale           | so a viewer's window maps to the same number of points on the Mac                      |

The other flags work as on Linux; `--audio-device-name`, `--microphone-fifo` and the
rounded-corner flags don't apply.

### Windows

voxl also streams a Windows desktop (Windows 10 or later), with every feature of the
Linux version (DXGI Desktop Duplication capture, SendInput, clipboard text and images,
WASAPI system audio). Build it with Rust, [vcpkg](https://vcpkg.io), LLVM (for bindgen)
and esbuild:

```powershell
vcpkg install x264 libyuv opus --triplet x64-windows-static-md
$env:VCPKGRS_TRIPLET = 'x64-windows-static-md'
npm install -g esbuild
cargo build --release
.\target\release\voxl.exe --port=6901
```

Open the link it prints. As on a Mac, voxl listens on `127.0.0.1` unless `--addr` says
otherwise. It streams the desktop of the session it runs in, so start it in the user's
session (not as a service); Windows hides the lock screen and UAC prompts from it unless
it runs as SYSTEM. For the microphone, install a virtual audio cable
([VB-CABLE](https://vb-audio.com/Cable/)): voxl plays into "CABLE Input" and apps record
from "CABLE Output".

| Windows flag          | Default                   |                                                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `--display`           | primary display           | display to stream, by index (0 is the primary); logged at startup  |
| `--audio-device-name` | default output device     | output device (name or prefix) whose sound to stream               |
| `--microphone-device` | first virtual cable found | output device (name or prefix) to play the browser microphone into |
| `--resize-scale`      | the display's scaling     | so a viewer's window maps to the same size on the desktop          |

The other flags work as on Linux; `--microphone-fifo` and the rounded-corner flags don't
apply. Dynamic resolution picks the largest display mode that fits the viewer's window,
and Windows restores the original mode when voxl exits.

## FAQ

**Why a WebSocket and not WebRTC?** One WebSocket goes wherever a web page does: through
reverse proxies, tunnels and sandbox preview URLs, with no TURN servers or UDP ports to
open. The browser decodes each frame the moment it arrives with WebCodecs, without
WebRTC's jitter buffer, and voxl runs its own rate control, which keeps latency low on a
clean link. The trade-off is TCP: on a link that drops packets (bad Wi-Fi, a weak mobile
signal) a lost packet holds up the frames behind it, where WebRTC can skip ahead.

**How is it different from Moonlight and Sunshine?** They're for playing games on your
own GPU machine through the Moonlight app, and for that they're the better fit. voxl was
built for things like software factories that use headless VMs and sandboxes (CI,
computer-use agents), usually on Xvfb with no GPU. It streams them to a plain browser tab
over one WebSocket and has APIs for agents.

**How is it different from RustDesk?** RustDesk is an open-source alternative to
TeamViewer and AnyDesk, for reaching your own computers or helping someone with theirs:
you install its app on both ends, desktop or phone, and the two find each other through
an ID server, then connect directly or through a relay. For that it's the better fit,
and it also shares Wayland desktops (experimentally) and Android phones, which voxl
doesn't. voxl is for desktops on servers, VMs and sandboxes: it's one process that
serves its own page, so there's nothing to install on the viewing side and no ID or
relay server to run. The stream goes wherever a URL does, can be embedded in another
page and comes with the APIs agents use. RustDesk has a web client too, but it still
goes through the ID and relay servers, and the self-hosted one comes with RustDesk
Server Pro.

**Why doesn't the stream load at `http://<ip>:6901`?** Browsers only allow WebCodecs on
HTTPS pages and on localhost. To watch from another machine, put voxl behind a TLS proxy
(Caddy, Cloudflare Tunnel, `tailscale serve`) and name its host with `--allowed-hosts`,
or forward the port over SSH and open `localhost`.

**Is it safe to expose?** voxl asks for a password by default but serves plain HTTP, so
put it behind TLS away from localhost. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

**Which browsers and devices work?** Any browser with WebCodecs, on an HTTPS page or
localhost:

| Browser                                                                | Works |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers 94+, desktop and Android      | Yes   |
| Firefox 130+, desktop                                                  | Yes   |
| Safari 16.4+ and any browser on iPhone or iPad (sound needs Safari 26) | Yes   |
| Firefox for Android                                                    | No    |

Phones and tablets get touch input and an on-screen keyboard.

**Wayland?** Not yet; on Linux voxl streams X11 displays, Xvfb included. The virtual
desktops voxl is built for run on Xvfb (E2B's and Daytona's do too), and X11 lets voxl
capture them without a permission prompt, with damage events that keep a still screen at
no CPU and power `/wait`. Wayland support is being worked on.

**Does it use the GPU?** Not yet. voxl encodes H.264 on the CPU with x264: 1.3–1.7 cores
for a busy 2560x1600 desktop, X server included (see the CPU table above). Hardware
encoding on macOS is in progress.

**What's the license?** voxl's code is MIT. It links x264, which is GPL-2.0, so a voxl
binary, and anything that bundles one, is distributed under the GPL.

repositories.name: e2e
repositories.description: Next generation e2e testing framework for web and mobile apps.
repositories.readme: # e2e [e2e](https://e2e.com?utm_source=e2e&utm_medium=github&utm_campaign=readme_intro) is an end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps. Describe a goal in natural language and an agent drives the app to reach it. Check the result with locators and assertions in the same test. ```ts // tests/checkout.e2e.ts import { test, expect } from 'e2e'; test('a member upgrades to Pro', async ({ app, agent, screen }) => { await app.open('/settings/billing'); await agent.act('upgrade the workspace to the Pro plan'); await agent.assert('the invoice preview shows a prorated amount'); await expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Pro'); }); ``` An agent step that a later assertion verifies records its actions, and the next run replays them with no model calls until the app changes. Tests without agent steps need no model. Bring your own subscription, API key, or local model. ## Quick start ```bash npx e2e init ``` `init` asks for an engine, web or mobile, and a model provider, then writes a config and an example test. The [quickstart](https://e2e.com/docs/quickstart) covers the rest. To see a finished setup in your stack, open [`examples/`](https://github.com/tester-army/e2e/tree/main/examples): Vite, Next.js, Astro, Angular, Expo, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Kotlin Multiplatform, Flutter, and .NET MAUI, each a standalone project with a passing suite. ## Packages ### Core | Package | What it does | | --- | --- | | [`e2e`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/e2e) | The SDK, runner, and CLI. | | [`@e2e-dev/web`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/web) | Browser engine: Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through Playwright. | | [`@e2e-dev/mobile`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/mobile) | iOS and Android engine: simulators and emulators through agent-device. | | [`@e2e-dev/decision`](https://e2e.com/docs/decision-models) | Decision-model executors for bounded semantic actions and assertions, and `decisionFilter()`, which leaves out the tests a pull request is unlikely to affect. | | [`@e2e-dev/acp`](https://e2e.com/docs/subscriptions#use-your-coding-agent) | Runs agent steps on your own coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) over the Agent Client Protocol. | ### Integrations | Package | What it does | | --- | --- | | [`@e2e-dev/kernel`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/kernel) | Kernel hosted browsers for the web engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/lightpanda`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/lightpanda) | Lightpanda, the open-source headless browser, started per run for the web engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/smol`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/smol) | smol machines browsers for the web engine: by default, each attempt branches a warm Chromium microVM. | | [`@e2e-dev/testmu`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/testmu) | TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) hosted Android emulators, iOS simulators, and real devices for the mobile engine, and hosted Chrome and Edge for the web engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/browserstack`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/browserstack) | BrowserStack App Automate real Android and iOS devices for the mobile engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/limrun`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/limrun) | Limrun hosted iOS simulators and Android emulators for mobile tests. | | [`@e2e-dev/eas`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/eas) | Expo Simulators hosted iOS simulators and Android emulators for the mobile engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/github`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/github) | Reporter that posts results as a pull request comment. | ## Documentation [e2e.com/docs](https://e2e.com/docs). The `e2e` package ships every page, so coding agents can read them offline in `node_modules/e2e/docs`. ## Join us Join us in changing how software gets tested. [We are hiring.](https://e2e.com/careers?utm_source=e2e&utm_medium=github&utm_campaign=readme_hiring) Questions? Ask on [Discord](https://tester.army/discord). Issues are for bugs and feature requests. Want to hack on e2e? See [Contributing](./CONTRIBUTING.md). We prefer an issue or a Discord discussion before a pull request. ## Security Please don't open public issues for security vulnerabilities. Follow [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md) and report them to [security@e2e.com](mailto:security@e2e.com). ## Telemetry The CLI sends anonymous usage data, such as which commands and engines run and where runs fail, but no test content, app content, or credentials. Opt out with `npx e2e telemetry disable` or `E2E_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1`. [Telemetry](https://e2e.com/docs/telemetry) lists every field. ## Status > [!NOTE] > e2e is in active development on the way to 1.0. APIs and config can still > change between minor releases.

> 🎨 **[Explore 50+ more open-source AI apps →](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/awesome-generative-ai-apps)** > 🤝 **New: [Open Duet](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet)** — open-source, self-hosted AI coworkers (named agents) with instructions, memory, routines, their own isolated computer, and your approval before they act. An alternative to Claude Duet, OpenAI Dots, and Manus Cue. [Star it on GitHub →](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet) ## 💰 Turn This Into Your Own Product — White Label & Resell Want to launch this as **your own branded AI studio** and charge your own customers for it? [MuAPI White Label](https://muapi.ai/white-label?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=open-generative-ai) lets you spin up a fully white-labeled version of this app — your logo, your colors, your custom domain, your own pricing — with zero infra to manage. You keep the markup on every generation; MuAPI handles the models, the queue, and the billing plumbing underneath. - **Your branding** — logo, color theme, and a custom domain (e.g. `studio.yourbrand.com`) - **Your pricing** — set your own credit/subscription prices for end users, keep the margin - **No infra** — no servers, workers, or model hosting to run yourself - **All studios included** — Image, Video, Audio, Lip Sync, Cinema, Workflows, and more, depending on plan Plans start at $49/mo. [Get started with White Label →](https://muapi.ai/white-label?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=open-generative-ai) ### What similar AI studios charge their users Consumer AI image/video platforms almost all run on paid monthly subscriptions — this is the same playbook you'd run under your own brand: | Platform | Typical subscription range | |---|---| | Midjourney | ~$10–$120/mo (Basic → Mega) | | Runway | ~$12–$76/mo (Standard → Unlimited), custom Enterprise | | Kling AI | ~$10–$92/mo across Standard → Premier tiers | | Luma Dream Machine | ~$10–$100+/mo | | Pika | ~$8–$58/mo | *(Figures are approximate, general-market ranges and change over time — check each platform's current pricing page before quoting them.)* With MuAPI White Label, you set these numbers yourself for your own end users — the subscription revenue is yours. --- ## API examples and model references - [OpenAI API examples](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/OpenAI-API) — GPT Image, Sora, and GPT endpoints through Muapi. - [Google Gemini Media API examples](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Google-Gemini-Media-API) — Nano Banana, Imagen, Veo, Gemini Omni, and speech endpoints. - [MiniMax Media API examples](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/MiniMax-Media-API) — Hailuo, H3 Max, speech, and music workflows. - [Kling Video API examples](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Kling-Video-API) — Kling text-to-video, image-to-video, and motion control. - [Qwen Image API examples](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Qwen-Image-API) — Qwen image generation, editing, and LoRA workflows through Muapi. ## Related Projects This is a curated set of high-value hubs, popular distribution tools, and model-specific integrations rather than a directory of every related repository. - [awesome-vibecoded-saas](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/awesome-vibecoded-saas) — broader catalog of open-source SaaS alternatives featuring this studio. - [Muapi open-source alternatives](https://muapi.ai/open-source/alternative/midjourney) — compare this studio with the Midjourney workflow and its honest scope. - [awesome-generative-ai-apps](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/awesome-generative-ai-apps) — catalog of open-source generative-AI applications. - [awesome-ai-video-models](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/awesome-ai-video-models) — compare video models by API, price, and capability. - [awesome-ai-image-models](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/awesome-ai-image-models) — compare image models by API, price, and quality. - [AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator](https://github.com/SamurAIGPT/AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator) — Open-source Opus Clip alternative application. - [open-duet](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet) — Open-source, self-hosted AI coworkers with memory, routines, isolated computers, and approval-gated actions. - [Open-AI-Design-Agent](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-AI-Design-Agent) — Ppen-source autonomous AI design agent. - [muapi-skills](https://github.com/SamurAIGPT/muapi-skills) — Agent-ready skills for driving generative-media workflows. - [Seedance-2.5-API](https://github.com/SamurAIGPT/Seedance-2.5-API) — Python SDK for Seedance 2.5 video generation. ## 🌐 Try it Online — No Install Required **Hosted version:** [https://muapi.ai/open-generative-ai?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=open-generative-ai](https://muapi.ai/open-generative-ai?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=open-generative-ai) Use all studios (Image, Video, Audio, AI Clipping, Vibe Motion, Lip Sync, Cinema, Marketing, Workflows, Agents, Design Agent, Apps, MCP & CLI) directly in your browser — no Node.js, no setup. Sign up for a free account to start generating. The hosted version is always up to date with the latest models. **Follow** the [creator](https://x.com/matchaman11) for updates --- ## ⬇️ Download Desktop App One-click installers — no Node.js or terminal required. | Platform | Download | |---|---| | macOS Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) | [Open Generative AI-2.0.0-arm64.dmg](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-Generative-AI/releases/download/v2.0.0/Open.Generative.AI-2.0.0-arm64.dmg) | | macOS Intel (x64) | [Open Generative AI-2.0.0.dmg](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-Generative-AI/releases/download/v2.0.0/Open.Generative.AI-2.0.0.dmg) | | Windows (x64) | [Open Generative AI Setup 2.0.0.exe](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-Generative-AI/releases/download/v2.0.0/Open.Generative.AI.Setup.2.0.0.exe) | | Linux (Ubuntu x64) | [`.AppImage`](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-Generative-AI/releases/download/v2.0.0/Open.Generative.AI-2.0.0.AppImage) / [`.deb`](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-Generative-AI/releases/download/v2.0.0/open-generative-ai_2.0.0_amd64.deb), or build locally with `npm run electron:build:linux`. | All releases: [github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-Generative-AI/releases](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/Open-Generative-AI/releases) ### macOS Installation Guide Because the app is not notarized by Apple, macOS Gatekeeper will block it on first launch. Follow these steps: **Step 1** — Mount the DMG and drag the app to `/Applications` **Step 2** — Open Terminal and run: ```bash xattr -cr "/Applications/Open Generative AI.app" ``` **Step 3** — Right-click the app in `/Applications` → click **Open** → click **Open** again on the dialog > You only need to do this once. After that, the app opens normally. **Alternative (no Terminal):** 1. Try to open the app — macOS will block it 2. Go to **System Settings → Privacy & Security** 3. Scroll down to find _"Open Generative AI was blocked"_ 4. Click **Open Anyway** → **Open** ### Windows Installation — SmartScreen warning fix Windows SmartScreen may show a warning because the installer is not code-signed: 1. Click **More info** on the SmartScreen dialog 2. Click **Run anyway** The app will install silently to `%LocalAppData%` with a Start Menu shortcut. ### Ubuntu / Linux Installation Linux artifacts are available when building with Electron Builder: ```bash # Build Linux installers (AppImage + .deb) npm run electron:build:linux ``` Generated files are written to the `release/` folder: - **AppImage** — portable, run directly after making executable: ```bash chmod +x "release/Open Generative AI-*.AppImage" ./release/Open\ Generative\ AI-*.AppImage ``` - **.deb** — install on Debian/Ubuntu: ```bash sudo apt install ./release/open-generative-ai_*_amd64.deb ``` If AppImage fails to start on older systems, install `libfuse2`: ```bash sudo apt install libfuse2 ``` #### Ubuntu 24.04+ / AppArmor sandbox restriction Ubuntu 24.04 and later enable a kernel security policy (`apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns`) that blocks Chromium's user-namespace sandbox. If the app fails to start silently or crashes immediately, you have two options: **Option A — Recommended: install the `.deb` instead.** The `.deb` package ships an AppArmor profile that grants the required permission automatically on install with no system-wide changes. **Option B — Temporary system fix (AppImage users):** ```bash sudo sysctl -w kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0 ``` This lasts until next reboot. To make it permanent: ```bash echo 'kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-userns.conf ``` --- Open Generative AI is a free, open-source AI image, video, cinema, and lip sync studio that brings creative workflows to everyone. Pick whichever fits the machine you actually run on: | Engine | What it is | Best for | |---|---|---| | **sd.cpp** (bundled) | C++ engine from [stable-diffusion.cpp](https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp), runs on the same machine as the app. Metal GPU on Apple Silicon, CUDA/Vulkan/ROCm on Linux/Windows. | Image-only models. Works on Mac M-series. | | **Wan2GP** (BYO install) | A user-installed [Wan2GP](https://github.com/deepbeepmeep/Wan2GP): either its folder on this machine (the app runs `wgp.py` itself) or its MCP server on another machine. Python + PyTorch on a CUDA/ROCm GPU. | Video models (Wan 2.1/2.2, Hunyuan, LTX-2) in **Video Studio** and large image models (Flux, Qwen-Image). NVIDIA/AMD GPU required on the Wan2GP machine; the desktop app itself can run on a Mac. | Both engines share the same UI: open **Settings → Local Models** to configure each. ### Engine 1 — sd.cpp (bundled) | Model | Type | Size | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | **Z-Image Turbo** ⚡ | Diffusion Transformer | 2.5 GB + 2.7 GB aux | 8-step turbo. Heavy on memory. | | **Z-Image Base** ⚡ | Diffusion Transformer | 3.5 GB + 2.7 GB aux | 50-step high-quality. Heavy on memory. | | **Dreamshaper 8** | SD 1.5 | 2.1 GB | 20-step versatile. Lightest tested option on Mac. | | **Realistic Vision v5.1** | SD 1.5 | 2.1 GB | 25-step photorealistic | | **Anything v5** | SD 1.5 | 2.1 GB | 20-step anime/illustration | | **SDXL Base 1.0** | SDXL | 6.9 GB | 30-step high-res | > **Z-Image models** require two shared auxiliary files (downloaded once, shared across both models): > - **Qwen3-4B Text Encoder** — 2.4 GB > - **FLUX VAE** — 335 MB **How to use:** 1. Open **Settings → Local Models** in the desktop app 2. Install the **sd.cpp inference engine** (one click — auto-downloaded) 3. Download your chosen model (and auxiliary files for Z-Image) 4. In **Image Studio**, click the **⚡ Local** toggle next to the model selector 5. Select your local model and generate — no API key needed All downloads happen inside the app. Nothing is installed system-wide. By default, `sd.cpp` stores the engine, model weights, and temporary downloads under Electron's app data directory. Common paths are: - macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/open-generative-ai/local-ai` - Windows: `%APPDATA%\open-generative-ai\local-ai` - Linux: `~/.config/open-generative-ai/local-ai` To keep multi-GB model weights on another drive, set `OPEN_GENERATIVE_AI_LOCAL_AI_DIR` before launching the desktop app. The app will create `bin/`, `models/`, and `tmp/` inside that directory, and **Settings -> Local Models** shows the resolved model folder. Local engine output and download errors are written to the app process console, so launch from Terminal or PowerShell when you need troubleshooting logs. ### Engine 2 — Wan2GP (your own install) The app does **not** bundle Python or model weights for Wan2GP. Install Wan2GP yourself on a machine with a CUDA or ROCm GPU: ```bash git clone https://github.com/deepbeepmeep/Wan2GP cd Wan2GP ./install.sh # or install.bat on Windows ``` **Same machine (recommended).** In the desktop app open **Settings → Local Models → Wan2GP**, set the Wan2GP folder (Python defaults to `/venv/bin/python`), click **Save**, then **Check** — it runs `wgp.py --dry-run` on a test task. Each generation runs Wan2GP's headless CLI (`wgp.py --process settings.json`); weights download automatically the first time a model is used, and the download shows up in the progress bar. **Another machine.** Start WanGP's MCP server there and put its URL (e.g. `http://192.168.1.42:7866/mcp`) in the same settings panel: ```bash python wgp.py --mcp --mcp-api-version 1 --mcp-transport streamable-http --mcp-host 0.0.0.0 --mcp-port 7866 ``` Use `--mcp-host 0.0.0.0` only on a trusted network (see Wan2GP's `docs/AUTHENTICATION.md` for OAuth/HTTPS). The Gradio web UI port (7860) is **not** an API and cannot be used here. Then switch **Video Studio** to **⚡ Local** and pick a model. Models your Wan2GP version doesn't have are listed with the reason; models whose weights aren't downloaded yet are marked. | Model | WanGP `model_type` | Type | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | **Wan 2.1 1.3B** | `t2v_1.3B` | Video | Lightest option, 480p, ~8 GB VRAM | | **Wan 2.2 14B T2V / I2V** | `t2v_2_2` / `i2v_2_2` | Video | 480p, slow on consumer GPUs; I2V needs a start frame | | **Hunyuan Video 1.5** | `hunyuan_1_5_480_t2v` | Video | 480p T2V | | **LTX-2 Distilled** | `ltx2_22B_distilled` | Video | 8 steps, 720p | | **Flux.1 Dev** | `flux` | Image | Image Studio | | **Qwen Image** | `qwen_image_20B` | Image | Image Studio | > **Why the remote option?** Wan2GP's runtime (Sage attention, flash-attn, AWQ/GGUF kernels) is CUDA/ROCm-only — there is no MPS / Apple Silicon path. The MCP server lets a Mac-only user keep the desktop app while offloading inference to a Linux/Windows GPU box, a gaming PC on the LAN, or a rented RunPod/vast.ai instance. > **Local inference is only available in the desktop app.** The hosted web version always uses cloud APIs. ### Hardware Notes - **sd.cpp** runs on CPU (all platforms) and **Metal GPU** on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4); CUDA/Vulkan/ROCm on Linux/Windows. - Metal GPU acceleration is built into the macOS desktop binary — significantly faster than CPU-only. - Recommended for sd.cpp Z-Image: 16 GB RAM (7.4 GB weights + 2.4 GB compute buffer). On a base 8 GB M-series Mac, **Z-Image is known to hang the system** — stick to SD 1.5 there. - For SD 1.5 on M2: expect ~1–2 s/step with the Metal dylib active. If you see ~10 s/step instead, the binary may have fallen back to CPU — see verification below. ### Verifying the SD 1.5 path (the fastest sanity test on Mac) If you want to confirm sd.cpp is installed correctly without going through the UI, you can drive `sd-cli` directly. This is the same binary the app uses. ```bash # 1. App data layout (created on first app launch) APP_DATA="${OPEN_GENERATIVE_AI_LOCAL_AI_DIR:-$HOME/Library/Application Support/open-generative-ai/local-ai}" ls "$APP_DATA/bin" # sd-cli, libstable-diffusion.dylib ls "$APP_DATA/models" # whatever you've downloaded # 2. Grab a small SD 1.5 model directly (Dreamshaper 8, ~2 GB) curl -L --fail --progress-bar \ -o "$APP_DATA/models/DreamShaper_8_pruned.safetensors" \ "https://huggingface.co/Lykon/DreamShaper/resolve/main/DreamShaper_8_pruned.safetensors" # 3. Run a single 512x512 / 12-step inference DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH="$APP_DATA/bin" "$APP_DATA/bin/sd-cli" \ -m "$APP_DATA/models/DreamShaper_8_pruned.safetensors" \ -p "a serene mountain lake at sunrise, oil painting" \ -o /tmp/sd15-test.png \ --steps 12 -H 512 -W 512 --cfg-scale 7.5 --seed 42 \ --sampling-method euler_a ``` A healthy run on Apple Silicon prints `total params memory size = 1969.78MB (VRAM 1969.78MB, RAM 0.00MB)` (Metal-backed) and produces a coherent 512×512 PNG. If `VRAM` is `0.00MB` instead, the dylib is CPU-only — check `otool -L "$APP_DATA/bin/libstable-diffusion.dylib" | grep -i metal` and reinstall the engine from **Settings → Local Models** if Metal is missing. --- ## ✨ Features - **Image Studio** — Generate images from text prompts (50+ text-to-image models) or transform existing images (55+ image-to-image models). 🔌 API Integration The app communicates with [Muapi.ai](https://muapi.ai?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=open-generative-ai) using a two-step pattern: 1. **Submit** — `POST /api/v1/{model-endpoint}` with prompt and parameters 2. **Poll** — `GET /api/v1/predictions/{request_id}/result` until status is `completed` Authentication uses the `x-api-key` header. During development, a Vite proxy handles CORS by routing `/api` requests to `https://api.muapi.ai`. File uploads use `POST /api/v1/upload_file` (multipart/form-data) and return a hosted URL that is passed to image-conditioned models. For multi-image models the full `images_list` array is forwarded to the API in one request. Lip sync jobs use the same two-step pattern: a dedicated `processLipSync()` method accepts `image_url` or `video_url` alongside `audio_url`, dispatches to the model's endpoint, and polls until the output video URL is available. ## 🎨 Supported Model Categories | Category | Count | Examples | |---|---|---| | **Text-to-Image** | 70+ | Flux Dev, Nano Banana 2, Seedream 5.0, Ideogram v3, Midjourney v7, GPT-4o, SDXL | | **Image-to-Image** | 70+ | Nano Banana 2 Edit (×14), Flux Kontext Pro, GPT-4o Edit, Seededit v3, Upscaler, Background Remover | | **Text-to-Video** | 85+ | Kling v3, Sora 2, Veo 3, Wan 2.6, Seedance 2.0, Seedance 2.0 Extend, Seedance Pro, Hailuo 2.3, Runway Gen-3 | | **Image-to-Video** | 120+ | Kling v2.1 I2V, Veo3 I2V, Runway I2V, Seedance 2.0 I2V, Midjourney v7 I2V, Hunyuan I2V, Wan2.2 I2V | | **Video-to-Video** | 35+ | Video effects, AI Clipping, Vibe Motion, video-conditioned edits | | **Lip Sync** | 15 | Infinite Talk I2V, Wan 2.2 Speech to Video, LTX 2.3 Lipsync, LTX 2 19B Lipsync, Sync, LatentSync, Creatify, Veed, Infinite Talk V2V | | **Body Swap / Recast** | 3 | Subject/appearance recast across image and video | | **Audio** | 15+ | Text-to-music, remix, and audio editing models | (Counts verified against `packages/studio/src/models.js` — total 420+ models across these 8 categories, plus additional models surfaced through Marketing, Agent, and Design Agent studios.) ## 🛠️ Tech Stack - **Next.js 14** — App Router, server components, fast dev server - **React 18** — Studio UI components - **Tailwind CSS v3** — Utility-first styling - **npm workspaces** — Monorepo with shared `packages/studio` library - **Muapi.ai** — AI model API gateway ## 🤔 How is this different from other AI Video Platforms?
